title: 3D-printed centrifugal compressor
short: An equation-driven impeller and volute modeled in SOLIDWORKS, simulated in ANSYS Fluent, printed in PLA, and checked against its predicted 24.55 CFM with an anemometer.
lede: A personal project that closes the loop between CAD, CFD, and hardware: design a parametric impeller, predict its flow, print it, and measure how far reality lands from the prediction.
ownership: Personal project. The parametric model, the simulation loop, and the anemometer validation described here are my own work.

results.label: Predicted volumetric flow rate from the ANSYS Fluent simulation
Measured airflow against the predicted flow, using an anemometer

sections.heading: Problem and constraints
paras: The compressor had to fit within its housing, targeting a **50 mm diameter** at **10,000 RPM**. Each blade's geometry depends on its neighbors, so a change to one blade ripples through the whole impeller.

sections.heading: Approach: equation-based blades
paras: Rather than sketching blades by hand, I defined them with equations. Varying the degree of power of a spline changes the blade shape, and the complexity of the model is set by the formula and technique used. The result is a parameterizable model that can be re-driven after each simulation.

sections.heading: Simulation feedback
paras: ANSYS Fluent simulations calculated the volumetric flow rate and visualized vortices within the volute, showing fluid stagnation and churning. Those results went back into CAD: I manipulated the design variables and resolved flaws in the parameterizable model.

sections.heading: Design decisions and trade-offs
bullets: Refining the blade equation improved geometric control, with a minor effect on performance.
Reviewing the model exposed design constraints I had not captured: zero-thickness geometry, conditions that cannot be manufactured, and insufficient design constraints overall.

figures.alt: Exploded grey CAD view showing the volute cover, impeller, and housing base separated along the axis.
figures.caption: Exploded view of the assembly.

sections.heading: Verification
paras: I validated the compressor with an anemometer. Measured airflow was within **±20%** of the predicted 24.55 CFM. That is a wide band, and the gap had identifiable causes: excessive shaft friction and PLA deformation, plus dimensional variation and unintended surface friction from 3D printing.

figures.alt: Green 3D-printed compressor housing held in a hand, with wires attached.
figures.caption: The printed PLA prototype.

sections.heading: Lessons and next steps
paras: The main lesson was the importance of design for manufacture. Next steps would be functional tolerancing, material selection for the application, and better drafting techniques.
